summary: Defines two RTCP Extended Report blocks for reporting initial synchronization delay and synchronization offset, for use in a range of RTP applications.

plainLanguage.summary: Two speakers must start together. These reports tell how long it took to get lined up at the start and how far apart they were.

questions: what is rtcp xr synchronization offset
what is initial synchronization delay in rtp
what are rtcp xr block types 27 and 28
how is rtp stream synchronization offset calculated
subtitle: Two RTCP report blocks that tell a sender how long a receiver took to line up its media streams, and how far apart they are.

tldr.problem: When audio and video (or layered video) travel in separate RTP sessions, a receiver cannot synchronize playout until it has the timing information for every session, and the streams can drift apart, yet there was no standard way to report either.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7244 defines two RTCP XR blocks: the Initial Synchronization Delay block (type 27), an average delay in units of 1/65536 seconds, and the Synchronization Offset block (type 28), a 64-bit signed NTP-format difference between a reporting stream and a reference stream.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can report both numbers so that managers can compare against targets and troubleshoot user-experience problems. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 7244 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the two synchronization report blocks.

sections.title: Two New Synchronization Metrics
sections.content:
This document adds two block types to the RTCP Extended Report (XR) framework of RFC 3611. The first reports the Initial Synchronization Delay: the time between the start of the RTP sessions and the moment the receiver has acquired all components of the multimedia session. The second reports the relative Synchronization Offset between two arbitrary streams, such as audio and video, that carry the same RTCP CNAME.

Both metrics are transport-level metrics in the sense of RFC 6792, and both blocks follow the guidelines of RFC 6390 and RFC 6792.
sections.plainLanguage: When music and a movie are played from two different places, you want to know two things: how long it took to start in step, and whether they are still in step.

sections.title: Why and When They Are Useful
sections.content:
A multimedia session is a set of concurrent RTP sessions among the same participants, one per media type. In layered video, each layer can have its own RTP session. A receiver joining such a session may not synchronize playout until it has received RTCP Sender Report (SR) packets on all components. For multicast, the Initial Synchronization Delay varies with the session bandwidth, the number of members and the number of senders. Without packet loss, it equals the average time to receive the first RTCP packet in the RTP session with the longest RTCP reporting interval. With loss, synchronization should rely on the in-band mapping of RTP and NTP-format timestamps from RFC 6051 or wait for the next SR.

Receivers can compare the delay with targets such as a Service Level Agreement. The offset block addresses streams that drift: the text gives an example of audio lagging behind video by multiple tens of milliseconds. A network manager can use it for troubleshooting and user-experience issues, and it also applies to one RTP session carrying several media types.
sections.plainLanguage: If the sound arrives a little after the picture, the show feels wrong. These reports let someone see that and fix it.

sections.title: The Initial Synchronization Delay Block
sections.content:
This block is sent by RTP receivers and needs to be exchanged only occasionally, for example once at the start of the RTP session. It uses block type BT=27, an 8-bit reserved field and block length 2. The SSRC of source is set to the SSRC carried in any arbitrary component of the RTP sessions in the same multimedia session.

The final 32-bit field is the average delay in units of 1/65536 seconds from the beginning of the multimedia session to the time RTCP packets are received on all component RTP sessions. The beginning is recommended to be the time the receiver joined the first RTP session. The value is computed from received SR packets or from the RTP header extension carrying the in-band RTP-to-NTP mapping. If the measurement is unavailable, the field MUST be reported with all bits set to 1.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a stopwatch reading: how long from joining the first stream until every stream was ready to play together.

sections.title: The Synchronization Offset Block
sections.content:
This block compares a reporting stream against a reference stream with the same CNAME. To make the numbers meaningful, a block for the reference stream with an offset of zero should also be reported. It relies on a Measurement Information block (RFC 6776) for the measurement period, SHOULD be sent in the same compound RTCP packet, and MUST be discarded if the measurement period did not arrive in that packet.

The block uses BT=28, the Interval Metric flag I, block length 3, the SSRC of the reporting stream, and a 64-bit Synchronization Offset. Here I=10 is interval, I=11 is cumulative and I=01 is sampled. The value I=00 MUST NOT be used, and a block received with it MUST be ignored.

The offset is computed like the Difference D in RFC 3550: D(i,j) = (Rj - Ri) - (Sj - Si), where S is the NTP timestamp of a packet and R its arrival time in NTP units. It is carried as a 64-bit signed NTP-format value with a 32-bit integer part and a 32-bit fraction. A positive value means the reporting stream leads the reference stream, a negative one means it lags, and zero marks the reference stream. If the measurement is unavailable, all bits MUST be set to 1.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick one stream as the leader. The report says how far ahead or behind the other stream is. Zero means it is the leader itself.

sections.title: SDP Signaling
sections.content: XR blocks MAY be used without prior signaling. To signal support, two parameters are added to the rtcp-xr attribute: rtp-flow-init-syn-delay for the first block and rtp-flow-syn-offset for the second. In offer/answer exchanges, the usage defined in RFC 3611 applies.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side can tell the other, before the call, which of the two reports it understands.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Two block types are assigned in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry: 27 for RFISD (RTP Flow Initial Synchronization Delay) and 28 for RFSO (RTP Flow Synchronization Offset). The two SDP parameters above are registered in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry, with the RAI Area Directors as contact.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers 27 and 28 and two short names were written in an official list so they stay reserved for these reports.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: When Secure RTP (RFC 3711) or other media-layer security is used, accurate synchronization offsets can expose details of the timing of the cryptographic operations. That might enable a side-channel attack on the encryption. Where this is a concern, implementations need to make cryptographic processing and media compression take the same amount of time regardless of media content. Apart from this, the blocks are believed to add no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 3611.
sections.plainLanguage: If the timing report reveals how long locking the messages took, a spy might learn something. Making every message take the same time avoids that.

data.title: RTP Flow Initial Synchronization Delay block

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: SSRC of source
fields.desc: SSRC from any component RTP session of the multimedia session.

fields.name: Initial Synchronization Delay
fields.desc: Average delay in units of 1/65536 seconds; all ones if unavailable.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: SSRC of source
fields.desc: SSRC of the reporting RTP stream.

fields.name: Synchronization Offset, most significant word
fields.desc: Integer part of the signed NTP-format offset.

fields.name: Synchronization Offset, least significant word
fields.desc: Fractional part of the signed NTP-format offset.
